clinicalPearls: Asymmetric oligoarthritis, predominantly of the lower limbs, arising 1-4 weeks after a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection
Classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and urethritis/cervicitis occurs in only a minority of patients — most present with incomplete forms
Enthesitis (especially Achilles tendon and plantar fascia) and dactylitis ('sausage digit') are characteristic clues pointing away from a purely infectious arthritis
Strongly associated with HLA-B27, particularly in cases following genitourinary infection or with axial/sacroiliac involvement
Triggering organisms include Chlamydia trachomatis, and enteric pathogens such as Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter
Mucocutaneous findings — keratoderma blennorrhagicum and circinate balanitis — can mimic psoriasis or STI-related dermatoses
Synovial fluid is inflammatory and sterile; cultures and PCR are negative for the triggering organism, distinguishing it from septic arthritis
Most cases are self-limited over months, but a subset develops chronic or relapsing joint disease, especially those who are HLA-B27 positive
harrison.pathophysiology: Reactive arthritis is thought to result from an aberrant immune response to bacterial antigens (or bacterial components/DNA persisting in synovium) following a distant mucosal infection, rather than from direct joint infection. HLA-B27 appears to shape the immune response to these triggering pathogens, promoting a sterile inflammatory synovitis, enthesitis, and mucocutaneous inflammation. It is classified with the spondyloarthritis family, sharing pathogenic overlap with ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis.
infectionMimics: Viral arthritis (parvovirus B19, hepatitis B/C, rubella)
additionalInvestigations: Synovial fluid analysis with cell count, Gram stain, and culture — to exclude septic and crystal arthritis
HLA-B27 testing — supports diagnosis and prognostic stratification, though not required for diagnosis
Stool culture or PCR for enteric pathogens (Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter) if diarrheal prodrome
Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification testing of urine/genital swab
Inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) — usually elevated but nonspecific
Blood cultures and gonococcal NAAT — to exclude disseminated gonococcal infection when presentation overlaps
Plain radiographs of affected joints/sacroiliac joints — may show enthesophytes or sacroiliitis in chronic disease
Ophthalmologic exam if uveitis/conjunctivitis symptoms present
redFlags: Fever with a hot, markedly swollen single joint — must exclude septic arthritis before attributing to reactive arthritis
Acute visual symptoms or eye pain suggesting uveitis — requires urgent ophthalmology referral
Signs of aortitis or cardiac conduction disease in longstanding HLA-B27-associated disease
Rapidly progressive axial disease or neurologic symptoms suggesting cauda equina involvement
Systemic sepsis features that suggest disseminated gonococcal or other bacteremic process rather than reactive arthritis
pitfalls: Assuming a sterile inflammatory joint effusion excludes infection without adequate synovial fluid culture and clinical correlation
Missing the diagnosis in incomplete presentations lacking the full urethritis-arthritis-conjunctivitis triad
Overlooking a preceding GI or GU infection because the interval before joint symptoms can be several weeks
Confusing mucocutaneous lesions (keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis) with psoriasis or sexually transmitted skin disease
harrison.prognosis: Most episodes resolve within 3-12 months with appropriate anti-inflammatory management, but relapses and progression to chronic spondyloarthritis occur in a meaningful minority, particularly HLA-B27-positive individuals. Chronic disease may involve persistent enthesitis, axial disease, or recurrent ocular inflammation requiring long-term rheumatologic follow-up.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Reactive Arthritis (Spondyloarthritis section)
management: First-line symptomatic control of arthritis and enthesitis with NSAIDs
Use intra-articular corticosteroid injection for persistent mono- or oligoarthritis, with a short course of systemic corticosteroid for polyarticular disease
Treat a documented Chlamydia trachomatis trigger (and the sexual partner) with appropriate antibiotics; antibiotics are not indicated for the arthritis following enteric infection
For disease persisting beyond a few months, introduce a conventional DMARD such as sulfasalazine, reserving TNF-alpha inhibitors for refractory chronic spondyloarthritis
Refer acute conjunctivitis or uveitis for ophthalmological assessment and topical therapy
Provide physiotherapy to maintain joint range and manage enthesitis
Monitor HLA-B27-positive patients for progression to chronic axial or peripheral spondyloarthritis
